title: Does Rogan Renewal Change The Bull Case For Spotify Stock (SPOT)?
detail:
Does Rogan Renewal Change The Bull Case For Spotify Stock (SPOT)?
Sasha Jovanovic
Mon, October 19, 2026 at 2:10 PM MST 5 min read
SPOT
Trade SPOT on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Spotify Technology renewed its multiyear licensing agreement with Joe Rogan and expanded its share buyback authorization by about US$1.5b to roughly US$2.22b, while investors look ahead to Q3 targets that include 788 million monthly active users, 305 million Premium subscribers and about €5.0b in revenue.

The combination of higher content commitments for a marquee podcast and a larger repurchase program highlights the trade off between audience reach, content spending and capital return as Spotify Technology works on margin expansion.

This raises questions about how Spotify Technology's broader investment narrative is affected by the enlarged share buyback authorization announced alongside the Rogan renewal.

Scan how Spotify Technology's latest Rogan deal and buyback compare with other platforms making bold content and capital allocation moves through our curated list of 20 high quality undiscovered gems.

Spotify Technology Investment Narrative Recap

For a shareholder in Spotify Technology, the core belief is that a huge global audience can be turned into a higher margin audio platform through better personalization, new paid features and a more efficient cost base. The Rogan renewal and larger buyback authorization do not fundamentally alter that story. The key near term catalyst still sits with upcoming user, subscription and revenue delivery relative to expectations, plus evidence that engagement tools like the Large Taste Model keep listeners more active.

The biggest near term risk remains pressure on margins as content, AI compute and marketing spend stay high while licensing costs to music labels remain structurally heavy. Higher commitments to marquee podcasts and Audiobooks+ can strain profitability if add on products, ad tools and ARPU focused features do not scale economically. The latest announcements mainly sharpen that trade off between audience reach and the timing of margin gains, rather than change it.

The enlarged share repurchase authorization, now roughly US$2.22b, is the clearest recent announcement connected to this news. It ties capital return more closely to the effort to lift profitability and free cash flow efficiency, including explicit 2030 margin ambitions, flatter headcount and higher revenue per employee. For you, the question is whether those efficiency gains and user monetization tools, from Audiobooks+ to AI remix features, can support that capital allocation plan without limiting core product investment.

It also amplifies execution risk around the podcast and audiobook push. Management is committing to both higher content obligations and a bigger buyback while analysts already flag about €200 million in incremental AI related operating expense in 2026. If new verticals and ad stack rebuilds do not translate into healthier margins on a reasonable timeline, the combination of richer content deals and share repurchases could leave Spotify Technology with less flexibility to adjust course.

title: Spotify Renewed Joe Rogan and Added $1.5 Billion to Buybacks. Here’s What Q3 Could Bring

Spotify Renewed Joe Rogan and Added $1.5 Billion to Buybacks. Here's What Q3 Could Bring ©cottonbro studio from Pexels and Bongkarngraphic from bongkarngraphic via Canva
Key Stats for SPOT Stock

Past week performance: +0.3%

52-week range: $405 to $697

Valuation model target price: $780

Implied upside: 47.0% over 2.2 years

Spotify Locks In Its Biggest Voice and Its Biggest Buyback

Spotify (SPOT) shares were essentially flat over the past week, up 0.3% to about $530. That calm hides a busy stretch for the audio streamer. Spotify renewed its deal with Joe Rogan, its most famous podcaster, and it expanded its buyback ahead of Q3 results on October 22. Investors seem to be waiting for proof before pushing the stock higher.

The Rogan deal is a new multiyear licensing agreement for The Joe Rogan Experience. Spotify keeps handling ad sales, while the show stays available on other platforms. Management did not disclose terms, but the deal reportedly mirrors Rogan's 2024 agreement and includes an estimated $250 million earnout. Retaining him protects engagement, yet it also keeps content costs elevated.

On capital returns, the board added $1.5 billion to the repurchase program, lifting total authorization to about $2.22 billion. A buyback reduces share count, so each remaining share owns a larger slice of profit. The program is discretionary, meaning Spotify can slow or pause it anytime. Its balance sheet holds about $7.4 billion more cash than debt, which leaves plenty of room.

Q2 gave management a confident backdrop. Premium subscribers reached 300 million, up 9%, while monthly active users (MAUs) rose 12% to 777 million. Gross margin hit a record 33.4%, and co-CEO Alex Norström told analysts that "Q2 was another quarter of healthy, broad-based growth." If SPOT stock is going to reclaim its highs, Q3 needs to extend that margin streak.

Spotify's Margin Expansion Is Doing the Heavy Lifting
SPOT Guided Valuation Model (TIKR)

Under valuation model assumptions realized through 12/31/28, the stock is modeled using:

Revenue Growth (CAGR): 13.9%

Operating Margins: 17.2%

Exit P/E Multiple: 35.4x

Based on these inputs, the model estimates a target price of $780, implying a 47.0% total return from the current share price of $530 and an annualized return of 19.0% over the next 2.2 years.

This is a margin expansion story first. Spotify's operating margin averaged a loss of 5.6% over the past three years, then improved to 8.7% over the last year. The model assumes 17.2% by 2028, which sounds aggressive until you check recent results. Trailing operating margin already sits near 14.6%, so the path requires steady progress rather than a leap.

SPOT Guided Valuation Model (TIKR)

Revenue growth of 13.9% matches the current pace. Q2 revenue rose 14% to €4.78 billion, and Q3 guidance of roughly €5.0 billion implies similar growth. Premium revenue grew 15%, while advertising grew just 1%, so subscriptions carry the model. For context, Netflix (NFLX) already runs above a 30% margin, showing how far a subscription media platform can scale.

title: We Don't Fear Market Corrections. Nor Should You.
detail:
We Don't Fear Market Corrections. Nor Should You.
The Rule Breakers Team, The Motley Fool
Mon, October 19, 2026 at 6:49 AM MST 4 min read
SPOT
NVDA
^GSPC
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

In January 2022, Team Rule Breakers recommended Spotify(NYSE:SPOT) to Stock Advisor members at about $209 a share. By November, with the S&P 500 deep in a bear market, it had fallen to about $69, a drop of roughly two-thirds.

Drops like that are hard to sit through, and with economic headwinds possibly ahead, plenty of investors are wondering how to prepare for the next one. Our answer comes from the philosophy by which every analyst on Team Rule Breakers invests. It starts with accepting that bad years will come, and it ends with a portfolio built to hold through them.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Spotify's story didn't end in November 2022, of course, and we'll come back to it.

Bad Years Are Part of the Deal

Down years are common. Depending on how you count, the market has fallen in somewhere between one year in four and one year in three. Some of those stretches have been brutal, from the dot-com bust to the financial crisis and the COVID-19 crash. Each one also turned out to be a stop on the way to the stock market's long-run gains.

So, at The Motley Fool, we don't try to call the next downturn. Nobody knows whether it will arrive next year or a decade from now, but history suggests it will show up regardless. We spend that energy studying businesses instead. A falling market sometimes offers great companies at better prices, and that's where our attention goes.

Built for the Drops

The Rule Breakers' habits and principles are built with these stretches in mind. The third habit of a Rule Breaker investor -- Invest. For At Least Three Years. -- sets three years as the bare minimum for holding a stock, and we'd happily hold our best companies for decades.

The fifth habit -- 5% Max Initial Position -- helps keep a single stock's fall from doing lasting damage to a portfolio. The sixth principle of a Rule Breakers portfolio -- Review Quarterly, Manage Accordingly -- has us checking in on each business when it reports results so that a rough week in the market doesn't drive our decisions.

Members who held Spotify through 2022 have since watched it recover. As of Friday's close, it's up around 156% since the recommendation, about 71 percentage points ahead of the S&P 500.

Know Your Own Timeline

Not every dollar necessarily belongs in stocks. The Motley Fool has said from the start that money in the market should be money you'd be comfortable leaving there for at least five years. That's the thinking behind the second portfolio principle -- Know and Name Its Purpose. A portfolio meant to fund a house deposit next spring has a different job from one meant to compound for 20 years.

Empirical research indicates that these revisions in estimates have a direct correlation with impending stock price performance. To capitalize on this, we've crafted the Zacks Rank, a unique model that incorporates these estimate changes and offers a practical rating system.
